content: The Commission on Accreditation of Medical Transport Systems (CAMTS) adheres to a set of industry-established criteria. As of June 2007, CAMTS accreditation has been granted to numerous programs in the United States, as well as three in Canada and one in South Africa. Background CAMTS first implemented its Accreditation Standards in 1991. These standards were developed collaboratively by its member organizations and through extensive public input and commentary. The standards serve as the foundation of the CAMTS program, emphasizing that the highest priorities for medical transport service providers are patient care and safety of the transport environment. Once granted, CAMTS accreditation is valid for three years, after which it can be renewed through a re-audit process. Preparing for initial accreditation typically requires four to six months, as the process involves a comprehensive review of all operational aspects, including management, medical protocols, and flight operations. CAMTS Member Organizations CAMTS is an organization of organizations, consisting of 14 member organizations, each of which has representation on the Commission's board of directors. These member organizations include: Aerospace Medical Association Air Medical Physicians Association American Academy of Pediatrics American Association of Respiratory Care American College of Emergency Physicians Association of Air Medical Services National Air Transportation Association National Association of Air Medical Communications Specialists National Association of State EMS Directors National EMS Pilots Association National Flight Nurses Association National Flight Paramedics Association Requirements for Accreditation Although CAMTS accreditation is technically voluntary, many government jurisdictions mandate it for companies providing medical transportation services as a prerequisite for licensure. This trend is growing as state health service agencies address safety concerns related to emergency medical service flights. For example, states such as Colorado, New Jersey, New Mexico, Utah, and Washington require CAMTS accreditation. Washington's rationale for adopting these requirements states that requiring accreditation of air ambulance services provides assurance that the service meets national public safety standards. The accreditation process is conducted by qualified professionals who assess air ambulance safety. Furthermore, compliance with accreditation standards is monitored continuously by the accrediting organization, and the standards are periodically revised to reflect the evolving nature of medical transport, incorporating input from various medical disciplines. Other states, such as Rhode Island and Texas, require either CAMTS accreditation or an equivalent demonstration of compliance. Texas, for instance, has adopted CAMTS' Accreditation Standards (Sixth Edition, October 2004) as its own. Operators in Texas who choose not to pursue CAMTS accreditation must undergo an equivalent survey conducted by state auditors trained by CAMTS. Similarly, Virginia and Oklahoma have adopted CAMTS accreditation standards as their state licensing requirements. Utah Controversy In early 2003, a controversy involving CAMTS led to a lawsuit. In December 2002, CAMTS withdrew the accreditation of Eagle Air Med, an aeromedical program operating in Utah that primarily served the Indian Health Service (IHS) on the Navajo Nation. The IHS requires its contracted providers to be CAMTS-accredited. During its application process, Eagle Air Med reported only one accident in its history, but CAMTS auditors discovered that the company had actually experienced seven accidents. CAMTS had previously suspended Eagle Air Med's accreditation twice due to safety concerns. When CAMTS ultimately revoked the certification, Eagle Air Med filed a lawsuit in January 2003 and requested an injunction until the matter could be resolved in court. In November 2003, a Utah district court ruled in favor of CAMTS, lifted the injunction, and upheld the revocation of the company’s accreditation. However, the court also ruled that Eagle Air Med could reapply for accreditation after six months.
